recognitions.title: This week, three separate claims of having fixed something didn't survive a single news cycle
recognitions.explanation: Across trade, foreign policy and debt management, the same pattern showed up: an announcement of control or resolution, followed within about a day by the other side, or the market, contradicting it. This week one of the three went all the way - the Canada 'deal' didn't just fail to hold, it collapsed entirely into real tariffs and real retaliation. A denial that talks with Iran even exist, followed a day later by a declared war footing against that same government. A bond-market intervention whose relief lasted less than 24 hours before yields fully round-tripped. The pattern isn't that these claims are false when made - it's that none of them are built to survive contact with the next news cycle.

evidence.text: Trump announced US majority control of Venezuela's oil reserves; within days, acting president Rodriguez was publicly insisting Caracas retains control of the resources - the deal's two co-authors can't agree in public on what it actually says, let alone anyone trying to verify it from outside.

Bessent unveiled sweeping new Iran sanctions Monday - 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting ~60 entities - declaring an 'ECONOMIC D-DAY' and claiming Iran is 'collapsing.' Tehran's national security chief immediately vowed to 'retaliate in a seismic manner,' and China called the sanctions illegal - the claim of collapse met by an unbowed, escalating counter-claim within the same day.

The story turned again: yields eased from a 19-year high of 5.31% (Aug 17) to 5.19% by Aug 26, real if partial relief from the buyback. Then Friday's Jackson Hole reaction erased it - the 10-year jumped 4bp and rate-hike odds surged - the fix keeps almost working, then getting overrun by the next news cycle.

recognitions.title: Three things that looked like resolutions this week all deferred the real question to later
recognitions.explanation: A ceasefire, a court ruling, and a shipping framework all landed this week wearing the shape of a resolution — and in each case, the people closest to it said out loud that the actual question is still open. A peace roadmap got its first verification mission, not a verified peace. A Supreme Court stay resolved a procedural fight while its own justices noted the underlying legality is untouched. A transit deal is 'in principle' and 'still being finalized.' Each is a real step. None of them is the thing a headline would make it sound like.

evidence.text: The administration just confirmed its own win is inconclusive: it filed a notice of appeal Friday against the Boston judge's separate nationwide block, sending the fight to the 1st Circuit - still fighting to make its Supreme Court victory actually change anything on the ground.

The shipping-corridor diplomacy is real, but Iran's own deputy FM undercut the 'resolution' framing directly: "The Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and any vessel passing through does so in coordination with Iran," with detention or confiscation threatened for violators. UKMTO confirms traffic remains significantly reduced - the corridor talk describes a negotiation, not the waterway's actual status.

Pashinyan's pivot got its form - a referendum plan, a bid in motion - but not its resolution: Lavrov himself dismissed the sequencing as 'sitting on two chairs' over $6B+ in EAEU trade, and Armenia's own Security Council chief now hopes Russia won't raise Kocharyan's case at all, tacitly admitting it's already on Moscow's table.
